label: Educational demos made to show an open-source tool. Not research.
what: How much survives of the ancient authors the Nobel Committee names in its 2026 bio-bibliography. Ancient testimony and modern estimates kept apart, as ranges, each with its sources.
reading_rules: Ancient counts are testimony (the Suda is a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia), not measurements.
Ranges mean the sources disagree; we never pick one number inside a range.
No single 'percentage lost'. The Sappho grid is labelled 'estimate' and names both totals.
'Survives complete' differs by author: Thucydides is unfinished; Sappho's one complete poem is short.

named_by_committee.phrase: tragedies such as Sophocles’s Electra (2001) and Antigone (2015)

ancient_count.text: 123, or more by some counts (Suda); 130 ascribed, 17 of them spurious, so 113 (Aristophanes of Byzantium, as reported in the ancient tradition)

modern_estimate.text: more than 120; no exact number is possible

survives.notes: plus about half of the satyr play Ichneutae, from a papyrus (more than 400 lines in whole or part)

ancient_count.text: 75 or 92, and 77 surviving in the Suda's day (Suda); 75 (Varro, in Aulus Gellius); 95 (some ancient scholars)

modern_estimate.text: about 90: 'approximately 92'; 22 productions of 4 plays give about 88

survives.notes: 19 attributed to him, 18 if the Rhesus (authorship disputed) is left out; includes the satyr play Cyclops

ancient_count.text: 90 tragedies (Suda); 70 tragedies and 5 satyr plays (ancient Life) and 73 dramas (ancient catalogue), as summarised by Ireland 1986

survives.notes: 7 survive complete; one of them, Prometheus Bound, is of disputed authorship, so 6 or 7

rows.author: Stesichoros

dates.text: c. 630 – c. 555 BC (Suda: born in the 37th Olympiad, died in the 56th)

survives.notes: only fragments, from quotations and papyri

rows.modern_estimate_note: No modern estimate of his whole output in lines was found; we give none.

named_by_committee.phrase: her interpretation of Sappho’s poem fragments

dates.text: c. 630 – c. 570 BC (Suda: born in the 42nd Olympiad, 612–609 BC)

source.name: Suda σ 107 (Sappho), Suda On Line, tr. E. Vandiver

ancient_count.text: nine books (Suda); the Alexandrian edition had at least eight books, the exact number uncertain

source.name: Suda σ 107 (Sappho), Suda On Line, tr. E. Vandiver

rows.author: Simonides of Keos

named_by_committee.phrase: the sixth century BC Greek poet Simonides of Keos

dates.text: c. 556 – 468 BC (Suda: born in the 56th Olympiad)

survives.notes: only a small part: fragments from papyri and quotations, and some short pieces whole; a papyrus published in 1992 (P.Oxy. 3965, the 'New Simonides', an elegy on the battle of Plataea) 'quadrupled' what we have (AGNI)

rows.ancient_count_note: The Suda lists his kinds of poem (laments, odes, epigrams, paeans, tragedies) but gives no count.

ancient_count_note_source.name: Suda σ 439 (Simonides), Suda On Line, tr. R. Dyer
ancient_count_note_source.paraphrase: The Suda lists the kinds of poem he wrote (laments, praise poems, epigrams, paeans, tragedies and more) but gives no count.

rows.modern_estimate_note: No count of his output was found; we give none.

rows.author: Catullus

named_by_committee.phrase: the Roman poet Catullus, with his famous elegy 101

modern_estimate.text: 116 numbered poems; 18, 19 and 20 are left out of most modern editions, so about 113 ('necessarily approximate'). A few lines quoted by ancient writers are not in the manuscripts, so some poems are lost.

survives.notes: Nearly all of them reached us through one manuscript, V, known at Verona around 1300 (c. 1290–1310) and lost before 1400; all complete copies date from the 14th century or later. Poem 62 also survives in a 9th-century anthology (the Codex Thuaneus).

rows.ancient_count_note: No ancient count of his poems was found.

shelf.label: one book of about 113 poems, through one lost manuscript

named_by_committee.phrase: she aligns the historian Thucydides with Virginia Woolf

ancient_count.text: 8 books by the usual division; some ancient readers divided it into 9 (Diodorus) or 13 (Marcellinus)

source.name: Diodorus Siculus 13.42, Loeb translation (C. H. Oldfather), LacusCurtius

modern_estimate.text: 8 books (a later division, not his own)

survives.notes: all of it, but unfinished: it breaks off mid-sentence in 411 BC, and the war went on to 404 BC

shelf.label: all 8 books, but it stops mid-sentence in 411 BC
